title: You can't subpoena a weight matrix

content: [▶ Scanner - Untitled (Mass Observation side A)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0gC4fJSm9vM&t=133)
2:13 of this song is sampled in 0:00 of the next song.
[▶ Bjork - Possibly Maybe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q3pavsAGTuY&t=0)
0:15 of the previous song is sampled in 1:03 of the next song.
[▶ DJ Shadow - Mutual Slump](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-6ycy0HjF58&t=63)

Bridging the concept of sampling in music to sampling in machine learning does not require an imagination nor a metaphor. For generative models, sampling is an important step at both training and inference time.
Music IP law is now quite established. If you sample someone's song without asking, it's up to that person to either ignore it or sue you.

But what if the interface for the sample is not a song, but an output (text, image, video, audio) from a model with no deterministic way to trace an output back to a particular source in the training dataset?

When models make inferences, the original training data which is prebaked into the generator is scrambled and reprojected into completely new sentences. The opacity is structural to the final, trained model itself. But what isn't opaque is the ground truth the generator is based on.
> "Hm, our generative model produces videos that are kinda like James Cameron's Avatar. Was this model trained on Avatar?"
With many of the most popular LLM providers, we can only guess.

AI companies may have stumbled into the perfect IP defense entirely by accident. In a typical IP suit, you have to show you own the original, that the defendant had access to it, and that what they produced is substantially similar to it. When the only user interface for the product is a stochastic generator, there's nothing to point to other than the probabilistic outputs it spits out.

**You can't subpoena a weight matrix.** And there's no deterministically traceable link between a training example and a specific model output. But you can subpoena the training dataset, and [courts already are](https://authorsguild.org/advocacy/artificial-intelligence/what-authors-need-to-know-about-the-anthropic-settlement/).
Generative models' responses come from 2 critical **ground truths**: the training dataset, and whatever context is passed as input at inference time.

If the model's ground truth (training data, feature data) is open source, we can trace an output back to original data with higher certainty. While you may not be able to prove a specific output came from a particular piece of training data, you can build a probabilistic argument that training on X influenced outputs that look like X. While an open dataset doesn't give you determinism, it does improve your confidence interval. A closed model confines us to observable behavior, where its internal structure and embedded biases [can only be inferred indirectly from outputs alone.](https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2025997928242811253)
You can only learn so much from shadows dancing on the wall.

> "Hm, our generative model seems to produce spot-on Warhol style paintings.", says Bill. Bill checks the training dataset, and finds that the model was trained on 10,000 samples of Andy Warhol paintings. He can say with pretty high confidence that the similarity of the paintings is due to the number of Warhol samples.
What if the dataset and the output disagree?

> "Hm our generative model produces songs really similar to Grimes and Bjork when I say 'produce a hyperpop track'", says Bill. Bill checks the training dataset, and he finds 3,000 other hyperpop artists who gave the owners of the model their data, but no Grimes or Bjork. He also checks the context the model had while generating the hyperpop song. No Grimes or Bjork.

> "Hm, our generative model produces prose that reads a lot like Philip K Dick's Ubik", says Bill. Bill checks the training dataset and Ubik isn't there. But 10,000 Reddit threads, Goodreads reviews, and literary essays about Ubik are. Did the model learn the book, or everything written about the book?
Where does this leave us? I don't know. I'm not a lawyer.

Is "he trained on 10,000 Andy Warhols" enough, legally and morally, even if no single output is a carbon copy? Is "the model's output looks an awful lot like my work" enough, legally and morally, even if there's no ground truth available? Should IP law be based on ground truth data composition or output similarity? Is this just a semantic similarity problem? If so, what's the threshold?

```
  Protected Expression              Model Output
  ┌──────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────┐
  │  Original Work   │◄── d(x,y) ──►│  Generated Work  │
  └──────────────────┘              └──────────────────┘

         Is d(x,y) small enough
       to constitute infringement?
```

In a generative model, an Amen Break sample dissolves into billions of floating point numbers and gets reconstituted probabilistically at inference time. There's nothing to point at if you're just looking at the output of the model. So, why would we _just_ look at the outputs of the models? The opacity of the weight matrix does not eliminate the traceability of the data distribution that produced it.

```
The Amen Break - "Amen, Brother" by The Winstons (1969)

  K       S     K K   S
  x . . . x . . x x . x . . . . .
  h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h
  ┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴
  1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a

  6 seconds. Most sampled loop in history.
```
